summary: Defines a MIB module for managing OSPF version 3, the IPv6 version of OSPF, so tools can configure and monitor it using SNMP.

eli5.summary: This is a dashboard of gauges and switches for watching and managing OSPFv3 routers.

questions: how to monitor ospfv3 with snmp
difference between ospfv2 mib and ospfv3 mib
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let management tools configure and monitor OSPF for IPv6 routers.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a standard way to configure and watch routers running OSPF version 3, the IPv6 version of OSPF, from a management system.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5643 defines the OSPFV3-MIB module, a set of SNMP-accessible tables and objects for areas, interfaces, neighbors and link state databases, plus notifications for important OSPFv3 events.
tldr.outcome: Any SNMP manager can read OSPFv3 state and change settings on a compliant router, and routers can raise throttled alerts when something goes wrong.

today: RFC 5643 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the OSPFv3 MIB Is
sections.content:
RFC 5643 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing OSPF for IPv6, known as OSPF version 3 (OSPFv3, specified in RFC 5340). MIB objects are normally reached through SNMP and are written in the Structure of Management Information, version 2 (SMIv2).

The fundamental mechanisms of OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328) carry over to OSPFv3, so this MIB follows the OSPFv2 MIB, RFC 4750, and includes REFERENCE clauses pointing back to the OSPFv2 specification where that applies.
sections.eli5: OSPFv3 is how routers share maps for IPv6. This document is the list of buttons and gauges that a person or program can use to look at those routers from far away.

sections.title: What Changes from OSPFv2
sections.content:
OSPFv3 differs from OSPFv2 in several ways, and the MIB reflects each one.

  • Interfaces: an OSPFv3 Interface Identifier is an IPv6 interface index, not an IPv4 address. The index of an OSPFv3 Interface Table entry is the IPv6 interface index of the interface OSPFv3 runs on.
  • Identifiers: Router ID, Area ID and Link State ID stay 32 bits wide but have no addressing semantics in OSPFv3, so they are typed as Unsigned32. A router running IPv4 and IPv6 can use a local IPv4 host address as its Router ID; otherwise it must be chosen another way, such as by an administrator.
  • Authentication and ToS: authentication was removed from the protocol itself, and Type of Service objects were dropped, so neither set of OSPFv2 MIB objects is carried forward.
  • Flooding scope: scope is now encoded in the LS type field, so the MIB has three link state database tables: Area-scope, Link-scope and AS-scope.
  • Virtual links: because router-LSAs lost their addressing semantics, a virtual link needs an Interface ID. A read-only object in the Virtual Interface Table shows it.
sections.eli5: It is like a new edition of a game with a few rules changed. The scoreboard had to change too: some old boxes were removed and a few new ones were added.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module is made of a general-variables group and a set of tables. The general variables are global to the OSPFv3 process. The tables are:

  • the Area Table, describing the areas the router takes part in;
  • the Area-scope, Link-scope (non-virtual and virtual) and AS-scope link state database tables, provided mainly for detailed network debugging;
  • the Host Table for configured host routes;
  • the Interface Table for IPv6 links running OSPFv3, and the Virtual Interface Table for virtual links;
  • the Neighbor, Configured Neighbor and Virtual Neighbor tables;
  • the Area Aggregate Table for prefixes that summarize routing information exported outside an area.

The Neighbor Table is read-only and holds what the router learned from Hellos. The Configured Neighbor Table holds manually configured neighbors for non-broadcast multi-access (NBMA) and Point-to-Multipoint interface types.

The module is registered as ospfv3MIB under mib-2 with the value 191.
sections.eli5: The MIB is a filing cabinet with one drawer for each kind of thing a router knows: areas, links, neighbors, and its big map of the network.

sections.title: Counters and Multiple Instances
sections.content:
The module defines several event counters, such as ospfv3OriginateNewLsas, ospfv3RxNewLsas, ospfv3AreaSpfRuns, ospfv3IfEvents and ospfv3NbrEvents. When reading counters, a manager should check the discontinuity object ospfv3DiscontinuityTime to see whether something happened, such as a restart of the OSPFv3 routing process, that makes earlier readings unreliable.

To manage several OSPFv3 instances on one system, the RFC points to SNMPv3 contexts, which can provide a separate MIB view per instance.
sections.eli5: The counters are like a car trip meter. If the car restarts, the meter may reset, so you check a note that says when that happened before you trust the number.

sections.title: Notifications and Throttling
sections.content:
Polling many routers to find a topology change is hard, so the MIB defines SNMP notifications for OSPFv3 events. The object ospfv3NotificationEnable gives coarse on/off control, and finer control uses the objects of RFC 3413. Defined notifications include interface, neighbor and virtual-neighbor state changes, configuration errors, bad received packets, link state database overflow, NSSA translator status changes and graceful restart status changes.

Three rules keep notifications manageable:

  • Ignore initial activity: a router should not originate the expected state-change notifications for an interface until two of that interface's dead timer intervals have elapsed.
  • Throttle: a sliding window caps notifications, similar to RFC 1224. A single window covers all types except ospfv3LsdbOverflow and ospfv3LsdbApproachingOverflow, which are not throttled. The RFC suggests 7 notifications in a window of 10 seconds. No notification announces that throttling began.
  • One per event: at most one notification per OSPFv3 event, carrying only the first unusual condition found.

ospfv3LsdbApproachingOverflow fires when the database passes ninety percent of ospfv3ExtAreaLsdbLimit. A manager may also poll the counters and enable notifications only when one starts rising abnormally.
sections.eli5: The router can ring a bell when something important happens. It waits a little at start-up so the bell does not ring nonstop, and it will not ring more than a few times in a short while.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects can be dangerous without protection. The RFC lists ways that improper changes could disrupt connectivity: disabling the OSPFv3 entity or an interface, deleting configured neighbors, lowering the limit on External LSAs, changing ASBR status, manipulating aggregation or metrics, changing Hello or dead intervals, or changing interface type. Disabling SNMP notifications can defeat remote monitoring.

Readable objects can expose the network topology and operating parameters, which could be used to target further attacks. Versions of SNMP before SNMPv3 lacked adequate security, so the RFC says implementers RECOMMENDED to consider SNMPv3 security features, and deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must also configure access so only legitimate users can read or change the objects.
sections.eli5: A control panel for a router should have a lock. Otherwise a stranger could flip the switches and break the network, or peek at the map.
